title: Methodology
text:
Primary: Was greater pre-pandemic dependence on international tourism associated with more severe 2020 GDP contractions among Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS small island developing states?
Secondary: Did the most tourism-dependent economies recover to their 2019 real GDP levels by 2022–2023?



This is a cross-sectional exploratory analysis. The unit of analysis is the economy (one row per country). The approach is descriptive and associational: we examine whether a pre-pandemic characteristic (tourism dependence) predicts an outcome (2020 GDP growth) using bivariate OLS regression and rank correlation.
This analysis does not establish causation. No controls for confounders (fiscal buffers, governance quality, pre-existing recession, pandemic response policy, population size, or economic structure) are included. The analysis is deliberately kept bivariate to maintain transparency about what the data show before additional assumptions are introduced.

title: Methodology
text:
Candidate Universe and SIDS Classification

Source authority
The candidate universe was constructed from the UN Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States (UN-OHRLLS) list of SIDS, retrieved November 2026 (source).


Classification categories








Category
Definition
N




OHRLLS-listed SIDS
Sovereign states formally listed as SIDS by UN-OHRLLS. Includes Cook Islands and Niue, which are sovereign states in free association with New Zealand and are not UN General Assembly members but appear on the SIDS list.
39


Associate Member SIDS
Associate members of UN Regional Commissions included in the SIDS group; mostly non-sovereign territories
18


Other island economy
BES (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba), retained for regional completeness; not on the UN SIDS list
1


Total candidate universe

58





Classification discrepancies documented

Cook Islands and Niue: Not UN General Assembly members. Included under “OHRLLS-listed SIDS” with an explicit note. No WDI coverage.
Bahrain: Not on the current OHRLLS list. Previously appeared on some SIDS lists. Excluded.
BES: Dutch special municipalities. Included as “Other island economy.” No WDI coverage, no OWID data. BES is the one candidate that appears in the universe but not in the analytical panel (57 economies in the panel, 58 in the universe) — because no data source produced rows for it.

title: Methodology
text:
Sample Definitions

Fixed-sample principle
Sample membership is determined by 2017–2019 indicator availability plus 2020 GDP growth availability. This definition is fixed and does not change when baseline windows are extended or narrowed. The 2017–2019 window was used for sample definition because it is the most recent pre-pandemic three-year period available for both indicators.


Four principal samples

Excluded economies (and why)
Economies not in any shock sample are excluded because they lack either: - A usable pre-pandemic tourism baseline (AIA, GLP, MTQ, MSR, BES, COK, NIU: no WDI coverage; BLZ, TCA: no OWID vspend data for 2017–2019). - 2020 GDP growth data.
Exclusion is based on data availability, not substantive selection. These economies are documented in data/processed/country_coverage.csv.

title: Methodology
text:
Baseline Windows

Two specifications








Window
Years
Rationale




Primary (2015–2019)
Up to 5 years
Broader window, less sensitive to a single atypical year; more stable estimate of structural dependence


Sensitivity (2017–2019)
Up to 3 years
Most recent pre-pandemic conditions; used for sample-membership definition





Transparency about window selection
The 2015–2019 primary window was evaluated after observing the 2017–2019 results. This is not preregistered research. The primary specification was not selected before examining the data. This is documented explicitly, and both specifications are reported in full (see Analysis, Table A5). The two specifications produce nearly identical results for the OWID indicator.


Baseline construction
For each economy and each indicator, the baseline is the arithmetic mean of available annual observations within the window. A country with 4 out of 5 possible years contributes a 4-year mean. Medians are computed as supplementary statistics (in output tables) but are not used as primary regression inputs.
No imputation. Missing annual observations are not filled. Economies with zero observations in a window do not contribute a baseline.


Thin baselines
Economies with only one annual observation in the baseline window are flagged as “thin baseline” in all figures (open circles) and tables. Kiribati is the thin-baseline economy in both OWID vspend samples (1 observation in both 2015–2019 and 2017–2019). Sensitivity analyses excluding Kiribati show minimal effect on results.

title: Methodology
text:
Shock Model Specification

Outcome variable
2020 annual GDP growth (%) from WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG. This is the percentage change in constant-price GDP from 2019 to 2020.
Limitations: - Annual GDP growth aggregates a full calendar year. Travel restrictions began at different times in different economies; some may have had partial within-year recovery. - GDP growth does not capture unemployment, poverty, or debt accumulation. - Some economies had pre-existing recessions that overlap with the pandemic period.


Explanatory variable
Pre-pandemic tourism-dependence baseline (% of GDP or % of exports), computed as described above.


Estimation
Bivariate OLS: gdp_growth_2020 ~ baseline_tourism_dependence
This is the simplest possible linear specification. No interaction terms, no controls, no fixed effects. This is intentional: the goal is to describe the raw association transparently before introducing model complexity.


Eight principal models



Dimension
Levels




Indicator
OWID visitor spending (% GDP); WDI receipts (% exports)


Sample
OWID shock sample; WDI shock sample; Common sample


Window
2015–2019; 2017–2019



Models 1–4 use the 2015–2019 baseline; Models 5–8 use 2017–2019. All eight are reported. No model is suppressed. Model preference should not be inferred from which produces the most significant p-value.


Multiple comparison adjustment
Holm’s step-down procedure is applied across all 8 principal p-values. This is reported for transparency, not as a definitive decision criterion. The 8 models are not independent (overlapping samples and related outcomes), so the Holm adjustment is conservative.


Influential observations
Cook’s distance is computed for all models. The conventional threshold 4/N is used to flag influential observations. Maldives (MDV) is consistently the most influential in OWID models (Cook’s D ≈ 0.36–0.39). Timor-Leste (TLS) is influential in WDI receipts models.
Excluding influential observations is reported as a labeled diagnostic sensitivity analysis. Influential observations are not removed from primary models. The Maldives is an economically meaningful data point — an economy with genuine extreme tourism dependence that experienced one of the largest 2020 contractions.

title: Methodology
text:
Coverage-Restricted Sensitivity
A secondary sensitivity analysis restricts each sample to economies with at least 3 annual observations in the relevant baseline window. This tests whether thin-baseline economies drive the results.
The most consequential case is S5 (WDI receipts, 2017–2019, WDI sample, N=35 → 21): 14 economies are excluded because WDI 2019 receipts data is missing (the baseline can only be computed from 2017 and 2018). The restricted N=21 sample still shows a negative slope (−0.143) but with weaker evidence (p = 0.055). This primarily reflects the severe reduction in sample size rather than an absence of pattern.

title: Methodology
text:
Recovery Index

Construction
Recovery_index_t = (Real_GDP_t / Real_GDP_2019) × 100
Computed separately for aggregate real GDP (NY.GDP.MKTP.KD) and per-capita real GDP (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD). A value of 100 means the economy has exactly returned to its 2019 level; above 100 means it has exceeded it.


Pre-pandemic baseline: 2019
The reference year is 2019, the last full year before COVID-19 travel restrictions. This is the most natural pre-pandemic comparison point. 2015–2018 observations are included to show the pre-pandemic trend.


Comparison year: 2023
The primary recovery comparison year is 2023, the most recent year with near-complete data for the sample (28/29 economies). 2024 data exists for 28 economies but is preliminary for some; 2025 data exists for 22 economies only.
Annual sample sizes vary across the recovery period and are shown explicitly in Figure 7. Cross-economy recovery comparisons at 2025 are not made because the 2025 sample (N=22) is not representative of the full shock sample.


Aggregate vs. per-capita distinction
These are not interchangeable. 19/28 economies recovered aggregate real GDP by 2023; 17/28 recovered real GDP per capita. The 2-economy gap reflects population growth in some Pacific economies. The Field Note reports both; claims about recovery should specify which measure is being used.

Missing Data

title: Methodology
text:
Reproduction

Software

R 4.4.1
Required packages: tidyverse, wbstats, here, scales, knitr, rmarkdown, patchwork, svglite



Script execution order
source("R/01_data_acquisition.R")   # ~2-3 min; calls World Bank API
source("R/02_data_quality.R")
source("R/03_preliminary_eda.R")
source("R/04_shock_models.R")
source("R/05_recovery_analysis.R")


Rendering the site
quarto render
This renders all four pages to docs/. The site is published from docs/ on the main branch via GitHub Pages.


World Bank API
WDI data is retrieved using wbstats::wb_data(). Future runs may retrieve updated data (particularly as WDI receipts lag resolves and 2025 real GDP estimates become final). The current retrieval date and returned codes are recorded in data/raw/worldbank/wdi_retrieval_metadata.txt. Note that ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS (tourism receipts) contains no observations beyond 2020 in this retrieval; this appears to reflect a change in UN Tourism data dissemination rather than a simple publication lag, and may indicate the WDI series is no longer actively updated.


OWID data
OWID CSV files in data/raw/ are fixed downloads from January–July 2026. They will not automatically update. To retrieve updated data, download fresh CSVs from the OWID grapher and replace the files in data/raw/.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Indicator Comparison








Figure 2: OWID visitor spending (% GDP) vs. WDI tourism receipts (% exports), 2015–2019 averages. The two indicators are correlated but not interchangeable — they divide by different denominators and measure related but distinct economic concepts.





The Pearson correlation between the two indicators (across economies with both) is approximately 0.77, and the Spearman rank correlation is 0.86. They produce similar rankings but material differences for some economies. The WDI receipts/exports denominator amplifies the apparent dependence of export-intensive small economies, while the OWID visitor spending/GDP denominator captures the share of overall economic activity attributable to visitors.

Recovery vs. tourism dependence

The absence of a significant association between pre-pandemic tourism dependence and the 2024 recovery index (Figure 6) does not mean tourism dependence was harmless or that the initial shock was inconsequential for these economies. Rather, the relationship between pre-pandemic exposure and longer-term economic recovery is not straightforward. Although tourism-dependent economies experienced particularly severe contractions in 2020, their subsequent recovery trajectories varied. By 2024, the degree of pre-pandemic tourism dependence alone did not explain which economies had regained their 2019 aggregate GDP levels.
Per-capita recovery provides a more nuanced picture. By 2024, 20 of 28 economies had recovered their 2019 real GDP per capita, compared with 21 of 28 for aggregate GDP. The difference illustrates why aggregate output alone can overstate the extent of economic recovery: an economy may regain its total output while remaining below its pre-pandemic level on a per-person basis. Population growth is one possible contributor to this divergence, although this analysis does not isolate its effects.

See Data Dictionary for source documentation and Methodology for research design.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
For most countries, a pandemic is a health crisis with economic side effects. For a small island economy built on international tourism, it is something else entirely: an abrupt, near-total halt to the primary source of income.
When COVID-19 closed borders in early 2020, international arrivals fell by roughly 74 percent globally. In the Maldives, where visitors routinely spend more than half the country’s entire economic output in a year, that collapse was not a disruption to one sector — it was a contraction of the economy itself. Across the Caribbean and the Pacific, islands that had spent decades integrating their economies around the movement of foreign visitors suddenly found themselves cut off from their primary engine of growth.
This analysis examines a straightforward empirical question: Were small island economies that depended more on international tourism before the pandemic more severely affected in 2020?
The short answer, for the primary measure used here, is yes. The more interesting question — what happened next — turns out to have a less tidy answer.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:

This analysis examines a straightforward empirical question: Were small island economies that depended more on international tourism before the pandemic more severely affected in 2020?
The short answer, for the primary measure used here, is yes. The more interesting question — what happened next — turns out to have a less tidy answer.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Measuring Economic Exposure
Before comparing exposure to outcomes, it is necessary to define what “tourism dependence” means. The answer is not as obvious as it appears.
Two main measures are used here, and they are not interchangeable.
The primary measure is international visitor spending as a share of GDP — the amount international tourists spend in a country relative to the size of that country’s economy. This comes from UN Tourism statistics, processed by Our World in Data (OWID). It is the most direct expression of how economically exposed an island is to the movement of foreign visitors: a high value means that a large fraction of economic activity depends on people who arrive from abroad.
The complementary measure is international tourism receipts as a share of total exports, from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI). It asks a related but different question: how important are tourism earnings relative to everything else the country sells or earns internationally? For export-intensive economies, this ratio can look quite different from the first measure.
The data for this analysis cover 29 in the primary sample — islands from the Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS (Atlantic, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean, and South China Sea) regions with both a usable pre-pandemic tourism baseline and 2020 real GDP growth data. These are drawn from a candidate universe of 58 small island developing states and associated economies identified through the UN-OHRLLS SIDS list.








Figure 1: International visitor spending as a share of GDP, 2015–2019 average. Source: OWID / UN Tourism; World Bank national accounts. Primary shock sample, N = 29. Open circle: Kiribati, with only one year of pre-pandemic data.





The range is striking. At one extreme: Aruba and the Maldives, with visitor spending averaging nearly 60 and 59 percent of GDP over 2015–2019. Antigua and Barbuda, Sint Maarten, and Seychelles were not far behind, all above 40 percent. At the other extreme: Guinea-Bissau and Trinidad and Tobago, where tourism plays a marginal role relative to the broader economy.
The differences matter because they translate directly into the scale of the exposure question. An economy where foreign visitors account for 60 percent of GDP is simply not the same kind of entity as one where they account for 5 percent — not in structure, not in vulnerability, and not in what it meant when international travel stopped.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
The 2020 Shock








Figure 2: Pre-pandemic visitor spending (2015–2019 average) vs. 2020 real GDP growth. Each point is one economy. The OLS line estimates the cross-sectional association; it is exploratory and does not establish causation. Open circle: Kiribati (thin baseline). Sources: OWID / UN Tourism; WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG.





The association in Figure 2 is visible without a regression line: the more an economy depended on international visitor spending before the pandemic, the worse its 2020 economic performance tended to be.
Fitting a simple regression across these 29 economies, each additional percentage point of visitor spending relative to GDP was associated with roughly 0.31 percentage points of additional GDP contraction in 2020. The relationship explains approximately 41% of the variation in 2020 growth rates across these economies (R² = 0.414, p < 0.001).
That is a substantial degree of predictability for a bivariate, cross-sectional relationship involving 29 diverse economies from three different ocean regions.

What drives this association, and what might complicate it
The Maldives deserves specific mention. With visitor spending averaging about 59 percent of GDP before the pandemic and a GDP contraction of roughly 33 percent in 2020, the Maldives is the most extreme observation in the sample — and the most statistically influential. Excluding it reduces R² from 0.414 to approximately 0.31, but the association remains statistically significant (p 0.002). The result does not depend on a single outlier.
The association also holds when:

The 2017–2019 mean replaces the 2015–2019 baseline (slope = -0.32, R² = 0.428).
The analysis is restricted to 24 economies with data for both tourism indicators — isolating the measurement from sample-composition effects (R² = 0.489).

This is an observational cross-sectional analysis of 29 economies. It documents that economies with greater tourism exposure tended to experience more severe contractions; it does not establish that tourism dependence caused those contractions. Confounders — pre-existing fiscal pressures, the timing of border closures, domestic containment measures, economic diversification — are not accounted for. The pattern is consistent with the economic logic, but consistent-with is not the same as established-by.


The complementary indicator tells a more ambiguous story
When the analysis uses the World Bank’s tourism receipts measure instead — receipts as a share of total exports rather than visitor spending as a share of GDP — the results are noticeably weaker. In the full WDI sample of 35 economies, the association is not statistically significant (R² = 0.1, p = 0.064). In the 24-economy common sample — the same countries analyzed with both indicators — it is moderate but marginal (R² = 0.233, p = 0.017).
The two indicators are correlated but not identical. They divide by different denominators and cover different sets of economies. Their divergence in results partly reflects those conceptual and sample differences, and partly reflects specific outlier cases — particularly Timor-Leste, which has high receipts relative to exports but experienced a less severe 2020 contraction than its tourism-receipts exposure would predict.
The full comparison of all eight regression specifications — two indicators, two samples, two baseline windows — is in the Technical Analysis.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Recovery: A More Complicated Picture








Figure 3: Real GDP trajectories, 2015–2025. Index: 2019 = 100. Each line is one economy in the primary shock sample, coloured by region. The horizontal line marks the 2019 level. Annual sample sizes (n=) appear at the bottom of each panel; they vary because data availability differs by year and economy. Source: WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD (constant 2015 USD). 2025 estimates are preliminary for a subset of economies.





By 2024, 21 of 28 economies with available data (75 percent) had returned to or exceeded their 2019 aggregate real GDP. The collapse and the rebound, for most of these islands, traced a steep V.
But the recovery picture is more textured than that simple count suggests.

Two kinds of recovery
Aggregate GDP and GDP per capita measure different things, and in small island economies, the gap between them matters. An economy where population has grown cannot treat a return to 2019 total output as a return to 2019 living standards; an economy where population has declined may show recovering per-capita output even when total output has not fully returned.
Of the 28 economies with 2024 real GDP data:

20 of 28 had restored real GDP per capita to 2019 levels by 2024 (71 percent).

The gap runs in both directions. Four economies — Seychelles, Antigua & Barbuda, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu — had restored total GDP but not GDP per capita by 2024. In the opposite direction, three economies — Curaçao, Marshall Islands, Tuvalu — had restored GDP per capita but not total GDP. These differences are consistent with the influence of population change on aggregate and per-capita output, although this analysis does not isolate population dynamics as a cause.
Seven economies had not recovered aggregate GDP to 2019 levels by 2024: Suriname, Cuba, Tuvalu, Trinidad & Tobago, Marshall Islands, Curaçao, Solomon Islands. For several of these, economic difficulties extended well before and beyond the pandemic itself.


Tourism dependence did not predict recovery
Here the story departs from what the shock analysis might lead one to expect. Among these 28 economies, pre-pandemic tourism dependence was not significantly associated with 2024 recovery (Pearson r = 0.21, p = 0.275).
This contrasts with the initial shock, where greater tourism dependence was associated with more severe economic contraction. Several highly tourism-dependent economies — including the Maldives, Seychelles, Bahamas, and Aruba — experienced sharp contractions in 2020 followed by substantial rebounds as international travel resumed.
The distinction is important. Pre-pandemic tourism dependence helps explain exposure to the initial shock, but it does not, by itself, explain where an economy stood relative to its 2019 GDP level four years later. Different recovery trajectories can produce similar endpoint results, and a single aggregate GDP index cannot capture the full economic experience of the intervening years.
This does not mean tourism-dependent islands recovered better, or were more resilient. It means that aggregate GDP in 2024 relative to 2019 is a limited lens for evaluating economic recovery. It says little about employment during the contraction, debt accumulated to finance the rebound, whether the quality of growth improved, or whether anything changed in the underlying structure of exposure.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
What This Adds Up To
The 2020 economic shock in small island economies was not random. It tracked, with considerable regularity, how much of an economy’s activity depended on international visitors.
This cross-sectional association — observed across economies as different as the Maldives and Papua New Guinea, Bermuda and Kiribati — does not by itself explain why exposure translates into contraction; that depends on fiscal buffers, economic policy, domestic alternatives, and factors this analysis cannot measure. But the association is strong enough, and consistent enough across different specifications, to be informative.
The recovery, by contrast, was not neatly structured by prior exposure. Most island economies found their way back to 2019 aggregate GDP by 2024. Some had not. The differences in recovery paths appear to reflect factors beyond the initial tourism shock — factors that vary from one economy to another and that a simple cross-sectional model cannot untangle.
Two things follow. First, tourism dependence is a meaningful indicator of exposure to travel-disruption shocks, but it is not a full description of economic vulnerability. Second, aggregate GDP recovery by a particular calendar year is an incomplete metric for evaluating how island economies fared through the pandemic and its aftermath.
The full picture requires looking harder at what happened in individual economies — not just at the pattern across them.

Long-format, unbalanced panel. 1,707 rows; 57 economies; years 1995–2025 (coverage varies by indicator and economy). UN SIDS count
UN-OHRLLS lists 39 economies under Small Island Developing States. Of these, 37 are UN General Assembly member states; Cook Islands and Niue are sovereign states in free association with New Zealand and are not UNGA members but ARE included on the SIDS list.


Bahrain (BHR)
Was previously on some UN SIDS lists as an AIMS economy. As of the current UN-OHRLLS list (retrieved November 2026), Bahrain is not listed as a SIDS. Not included in the candidate universe.


Associate Members
The 18 associate members listed by UN-OHRLLS are territories and dependencies that are associate members of UN Regional Commissions. They are included in the SIDS group but are not sovereign states. Not all have WDI coverage.


BES
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are Dutch special municipalities. Not on the UN-OHRLLS list. Retained in the candidate universe as an other island economy for regional completeness. No WDI coverage and does not contribute to any analytical sample.
